findings: NOTE (rebuilt option C): refuted by displacement plus arithmetic vouching rather than by direct contradiction, which is a shade softer than the flat inversions carried by A and D in the same question. Judged sufficient, reasoning in the justification.
justification: A at full strength: the second sentence puts 1931 in play ('The weir held water for a mill that stopped in 1931'), a mill closing is exactly the event that starts a logbook, and 'the mill that the weir was built to serve' is a natural gloss on 'held water for'. Refuted by the next sentence, which dates the book outright - 'Since the pass opened in 2011 the trap has been emptied most mornings of the run, the counts written into a hardbacked book' - and by the fact that the trap sits in the pass, which did not exist before 2011; fifteen springs from 2011 also reconciles with 'Over fifteen springs the book records'. C at full strength (REBUILT, judged as new work): the passage does single out the early record as different in kind ('The first nine springs are in one hand, the rest in three others'), the tally is lopsided in exactly the way a recording error would produce ('31 dace and nine chub'), dace and chub are both silvery cyprinids that are genuinely confusable in the hand, and the story would neatly dissolve the article's central puzzle - few dace in the book, a river below 'thick with dace'. Against: nothing in the text touches the recorders' competence, the one-hand sentence is about custody and handwriting only, and two things displace the option. First, the article supplies an evidenced rival explanation - the tag study finds the dace physically do not enter, 'Twenty-three of the 174 crossed the antenna on the left bank... Nine went in' - which a recording error would not produce. Second, and more decisively, the narrator computes with the book's dace figure and finds it coherent: 'Five came out at the top, a sixth of all the dace in the book' - five is a sixth of thirty-one, so the text affirmatively vouches for the very number C says is corrupt. That is refutation by the passage's own use of the datum rather than by a contradicting sentence, and I record it as the softest refutation in this question while judging it sufficient: a student who picks C can be shown both spans. D at full strength: a hurried reader parses 'one hand ... three others' knowing there are four hands and attaches the three to the nine springs, which feels right because nine of fifteen is the majority; the option is also arithmetically consistent with a total of four keepers, so it feels checked. Flatly inverted by the same sentence. All three refutable.

A at full strength, and this is the strongest distractor in the unit because the narrator arms it: Kelsingham herself downgrades the result - 'The temperature split she calls suggestive and no more' - and eleven fish above ten degrees is a sample a careful reader is right to distrust, so a sceptic can conclude the difference is not real. Refuted because 'suggestive and no more' governs inferential weight, not the numbers, and the stem asks what we are told: 'Of the eleven that entered above ten degrees, seven got out; of the twenty-eight that entered colder, five did' is 64 per cent against 18. The option teaches the difference between an uncertain effect and an absent one. B at full strength: a nine-walled pool-and-weir pass IS a resting ladder by design, and the passage supplies the stepped structure ('the fall from one pool to the next about 270 millimetres') whose whole point is to break the head into rests, so a reader importing standard design intent gets B honestly. Refuted flatly and at this structure specifically: 'The pools do not help. They are short, and at April flows the jet from one notch reaches the wall of the next; there is no quiet corner in them.' C at full strength: grayling are larger than the dace the previous paragraph watched fail, so a reader carrying that frame forward expects size to be the operative variable, and 'deep through the body' is easy to file under size. Refuted because the passage names shape and only shape - 'deep through the body and carries a dorsal fin like a sail, and it does not leave the water' - and never mentions grayling size at all; C's 'rather than' makes it a direct denial of the stated cause, so it is refuted rather than merely unsupported.

B at full strength: this is the explanation the article says people reach for first, and it has real footing in the passage's own numbers - a 2.4 metre head against a fish the text itself calls small ('a dace is a small fish'). Refuted by the stem's voice requirement plus 'thinks strength has little to do with it', with the 270 millimetre step given to show how small the demand is. C at full strength: the passage establishes run-timing as a live category ('the trout, which run in November and December'), 'most mornings of the run' implies an operating season, and the word 'opened' appears attached to the pass ('Since the pass opened in 2011'), so a reader has the materials to build a seasonal-gate story. Refuted because 'opened' there means commissioned, the pass is an ungated concrete chute throughout, and the tag data disproves a timing miss directly: dace reached the weir while the pass was live - 'Within nine days 174 of them had been read at the weir' - and nine entered it. D at full strength, and this is the best distractor in the unit: the passage makes shoaling the defining behavioural fact about dace ('They move up in loose shoals along the margins'), a notched chute admits fish essentially singly, and the numbers fit a cohesion story perfectly - 174 at the weir, only nine in. Refuted because the passage assigns shoaling a different job, explaining where the dace travel rather than whether they will enter, and Kelsingham rules out reluctance in her own words: 'The dace aren't beaten by the ladder. They don't find it, and they don't find it because they don't come up that side of the river.' Not finding is not refusing, and the nine that entered did so singly with five getting out, so individual ascent is demonstrated. A real passage fact turned to a wrong purpose - the misconception worth teaching.

findings: NOTE (rebuilt option A): the closest call in the unit. A's falsity rests on reading 'is what packed' as a claim about the differentiating cause; under a loose restatement reading ('a spate packed it') a student could think it true. Judged controlled by the stem's 'implied' and by C standing beside it as the rival explanation of the same contrast, so no flag.

NOTE (rebuilt option D): successful rebuild - now doubly refuted, on wall count and on current state. Its scope overreach is somewhat visible without the passage (recorded under G-STEM), which is the ordinary trade for buying refutability.
justification: A at full strength (REBUILT, judged as new work): the passage says in as many words that a spate did it - 'A spate in February packed the lower one to the top with gravel' - so A reads as a near-quotation, and it is physically sensible, since spates are what mobilise bed material. Refuted by the sentence immediately after the one it quotes: 'The other, three walls further up, came through the same water clear.' The passage deliberately holds the hydraulics constant across the two orifices, so the spate's force is the common condition and cannot be the differentiating cause; a cause present in both cases explains neither difference. Note that A is not merely off-target but false: 'is what packed' asserts sufficiency, and the same water failing to pack the upper orifice falsifies sufficiency. B at full strength, and it is genuinely tempting for the engaged reader: a submerged orifice really does bleed flow that would otherwise cross the notch, and reducing notch velocity is a standard way to make a pass passable for weaker swimmers - which the passage has already established as the grayling's obstacle, 'to get up a notch it must swim through the jet'. A reader who has absorbed that finds B better motivated than the real purpose. Refuted on the stated purpose clause: 'so a fish could go through a wall instead of over it' is a route purpose, not a flow purpose. It punishes substituting your own better engineering for the text's stated intent. D at full strength (REBUILT): the passage's stated purpose is exactly the language D uses, 'go through a wall instead of over it', so a reader who generalises from stated intent to achieved result lands here with the passage's own words. Refuted twice and independently - on count, 'In 2023 two of the nine cross-walls were cut', which leaves seven walls crossable only by the notch so that 'the whole pass' is impossible; and on state, 'A spate in February packed the lower one to the top with gravel, and it is still packed', which reduces the two to one. Both rebuilds achieve refutability from locatable spans.

A at full strength: the piece is built on counts of fish that did and did not pass a weir ('6,140 brown trout, 288 grayling, 31 dace and nine chub'), so the first half is a fair description of the raw material, and a reader may take the upstream consequence as the obvious unstated stake. Refuted by absence of subject, which is the correct refutation form for a main-idea option: the reach above the weir is never described, sampled or discussed, and the article states its own interest elsewhere - 'What has taken fifteen years to become interesting is what it works for.' B at full strength, and it is the most seductive of the three because it is nearly right in shape: the article really is organised around counts, and it really does end up asking what a pass delivers by species rather than whether it works in the abstract. Refuted because the counts pose the problem rather than support a case - 'Nobody says the pass does not work' concedes the throughput point instead of arguing it - and because the argumentative work is done by tagging and by where fish put themselves in moving water, which is mechanism, not a criterion of judgement; the piece never advocates a general way of judging passes. C at full strength: the article does close on remediation and does report failure ('it is still packed'), and names a further remedy, 'a second mouth on the right bank'; a reader who weights endings gets C, whose second half is genuinely true of the 2023 orifices. Refuted on proportion - the remedial work is the final three sentences of a seven-paragraph piece whose body is a study of why two species fail - and on scope, since 'what is being done' overstates one 2023 trial plus one unbuilt proposal.

findings: NOTE (sub-threshold, not a defect): the passage attributes the soaking specifically to the plasticiser but the translucency to 'the glue' going in; option C follows the passage's looser 'adhesive' phrasing while option A tests the rubber/plasticiser split. C is directly supported by the passage's own clause, so this is recorded as a small internal tension in the conservator's spoken register, not as an error.
justification: MECHANISM VERIFICATION after the paragraph interleave - all five steps present, in order, and none orphaned from its subject. Carrier fails: 'Three flakes of film clung along one edge' and 'Mostly there's no tape left; the film let go years ago'. Adhesive stays: 'What's left is the glue.' Plasticiser migrates: 'the plasticiser that kept it soft has soaked into the paper'. Rubber oxidises to give the brown: 'The rubber in it has oxidised - that's the brown'. Heat lifts fresh, aged needs solvent: 'She warms a mend from last year, and the film lifts and brings most of the glue with it. On a mend as old as this one, heat does nothing. The glue has gone hard, she says, so only a solvent will move it.' The inserted narration beat 'She turns the certificate to the light.' falls between the 'what's left is the glue' turn and the chemistry turn, so it separates two complete quoted units rather than splitting a mechanism step; the fresh-mend demonstration and the aged-mend contrast remain adjacent in paragraph 3, where the contrast has to live. Mechanism reads correctly. A at full strength: both nouns are on the page doing something to the paper, the plasticiser is the component said to enter the sheet ('has soaked into the paper') and the brown is in the sheet ('The brown that's in the fibres'), so plasticiser-in-paper and brown-in-fibres line up geographically, and the temporal clause is true since the film did come away. A well-built swap. Refuted by the appositive that leaves no room: 'The rubber in it has oxidised - that's the brown', with the plasticiser given the other job in the same sentence, and soaking is not oxidising. B at full strength: folk chemistry assigns solvent to hardened residue and heat to softening, and the sentence order helps the error, since the warming sentence precedes the words 'gone hard'. Refuted by a demonstration that runs explicitly the other way across three sentences of paragraph 3. D at full strength, and it is the most charitable error available: the passage does establish solvent-matching as the real technique ('which solvent depends on what the glue was made of'), and the stain is a residue of the same adhesive system, so extending the solvent's success to it is reasoning, not carelessness. Refuted by the flagged hedge: 'About the stain itself she is careful: The brown that's in the fibres I can lighten. I don't promise to take it out.' Lighten, not remove, and the refusal is explicit - it teaches reading a professional's careful limit as load-bearing.

ARITHMETIC RECONCILIATION, both routes, and they are independent. Route 1 (direct): 74 applicants, 'Sjuttiofyra sökte plats till den marknaden', minus 58 placed, 'alla femtioåtta stånd var upptagna när den öppnade', leaves 16 without a place. Route 2 (via vacancies): capacity 58, 'Torget rymmer femtioåtta stånd'; 4 fell vacant, 'Fyra platser blev lediga inför förra höstens marknad', so 54 incumbents renewed under 'den som stod på torget året innan får stå där igen'; the 74 therefore comprise 54 incumbents and 20 newcomers, and 20 newcomers for 4 vacancies leaves 16 turned away. Route 1 never uses the vacancy figure and route 2 never subtracts 58 from 74, so the agreement at 16 is a real check. The reference class cannot slide: 'Alla som vill ha plats måste söka varje år' forces the 74 to be the whole pool including incumbents, and the only competing reading, 74 as newcomers only, would put 54 + 74 = 128 applicants against a stated 74 and yield 70 unplaced. It is also confirmed that no incumbent can be among the 16, since the renewal rule guarantees a returning holder a place, so the 16 are exactly the unsuccessful newcomers and 'de sökande' in option D refers unambiguously to the 74. A at full strength: the passage establishes annual re-application and oversubscription, which is precisely the setup a lottery solves, and Swedish market and allotment schemes commonly do allocate by lot, so a reader supplying the ordinary institutional solution gets A. Refuted by the contrastive second half of the very sentence its premise comes from: 'men den som stod på torget året innan får stå där igen'. B at full strength: the number four is live two sentences away ('Fyra platser blev lediga'), and plats 1 is the one pitch singled out for description and the most desirable one, the corner by the pharmacy, which is where turnover stories naturally attach. Refuted twice - the number is misattached, and the claim is inverted by 'står i Gottfrid Runessons namn och har gjort det längre än platskartan går tillbaka'. C at full strength: 'Alla som vill ha plats måste söka varje år' reads on its own as an equal-footing rule under which incumbency confers nothing, and a scarce market might well rotate its pitches. Refuted by the same 'men' clause that kills A, from the opposite direction, with the consequence visible in the vacancy count of four. A and C form a clean pair of opposite errors about one rule.

B at full strength, and it is the best distractor in the unit because the article itself points at it: the writer concedes the two-day requirement is the hard objection - 'på fältet skulle marknaden hållas två dagar, och platsen betalas per dag. Fyrtiotre av de femtioåtta stånden på torget sköts av en enda människa. Den som står ensam kan inte stå två dagar, och då blir den andra dagen ingen ny handel utan en avgift till' - and then admits 'Det svaret har jag inte.' A reader who treats that admission as decisive builds the obvious compromise, which is also the most reasonable position in the text's own terms. Refuted because she does not adopt it: 'Flytta hela marknaden, båda dagarna, från och med nästa höst', where 'båda dagarna' refuses exactly this, and because 'Det svaret har jag inte' concedes she cannot rebut the objection, not that she yields to it. C at full strength: she grants the majority's case in unusually strong terms, 'De trettionio har två skäl, och båda håller', concedes she has no answer to the second, and volunteers that her own motive is self-interested - 'flyttar marknaden ut, tjänar jag på det. Det gör inte de flesta andra' - which a reader may take as self-disqualification. Refuted by her declared side in the first paragraph, 'Jag var en av de tolv', and by the imperative coda; the concessions are the rhetoric of a fair-minded minority, not a change of position. D at full strength: she concedes the first years will be worse - 'De första åren blir sämre. Ingen som räknar kommer fram till något annat' - which is exactly the situation a trial period exists to manage, and a trial is the standard way an association settles a split vote. Refuted by name and with a reason: 'Ett provår vill jag ändå inte ha', because 'folk måste hinna vänja sig vid att åka dit'. All three distractors are refuted rather than merely unsupported, and each carries a distinct misreading - compromise mistaken for position, concession mistaken for agreement, and problem mistaken for proposal.

B at full strength: a formal parlour is, on most readers' models, the room you show your best company into, and the passage does present it as the room of honour - 'här fanns utrymme att avvara och något att visa den som kom utifrån' - so the ordinary domestic logic delivers B. Refuted three times: the criterion is denied outright in the paragraph's opening clause, 'avgjordes inte av hur nära man stod varandra', and the counter-cases are supplied in 'Grannar och släkt satt i köket, oavsett hur långt de hade rest' and 'Den som stod hushållet närmast kom sällan längre än till köksbordet'. C at full strength, and this is an intelligent inference rather than a careless one: a room that must be heated before use - 'Kaminen eldades först när rummet skulle användas' - practically requires notice, so the stove detail genuinely licenses an appointment system. Refuted by a purpose-built span: 'Sköterskan var oanmäld varannan gång och visades in ändå', where 'ändå' marks the sentence as answering exactly this inference. D at full strength, and it is the strongest here because its extension very nearly coincides with the key's: in a forest parish the priest, the district nurse and the forest valuer are the three figures of highest standing, so a reader who induces from the list rather than from the stated rule gets D with the list on their side. Refuted by the stated criterion, 'utan av vad besöket gällde', and by the discriminating case the passage plants for it: a hired man come to value timber is admitted while the neighbour from the house next door 'blev stående i farstun med mössan i handen'. If rank governed, a valuer would not outrank a neighbouring farmer. A distractor whose extension nearly matches the key's, separated by one deliberately placed example, is the construction that actually teaches criterion-reading.

A at full strength, and it is well grounded: the passage says the door closed again exactly as before, 'Dörren till finrummet gick igen som förut', and that the suite never moved, 'Samma soffgrupp står kvar hos honom'. A room whose door shut and whose furniture stayed put is, on any ordinary reading, untouched. Refuted by the sentence placed immediately after those supports: 'Hemma hos oss stod farfars kista i finrummet flera år efter att vår apparat hade burits ut.' The room went on serving its heaviest use after the set left, so the general claim 'orört' is falsified by a stated instance - and the option's generality is precisely what makes it wrong. The placement is deliberate and good: the reader who stops one sentence early gets A. B at full strength: a front room brought into daily use by a television is exactly where furniture turnover happens, and the passage does record the room furnished for sitting ('en soffgrupp') and sat in ('de satt i ytterrock framför den'), so a reader modelling the ordinary trajectory supplies replacement furniture. Refuted flatly by 'Samma soffgrupp står kvar hos honom', in the same paragraph as the television - the least tempting of the three, but sound. D at full strength: the passage's other spans are long, the wait for a rural house to get central heating sounds long, and 'tre vintrar' counts winters rather than years, which a skimmer may not register as a total. Refuted on the stated count: 'Hos Hilding Wibbelund stod den i tre vintrar innan huset fick element', followed by 'Sen bar far ut den i köket'. Three, not more than ten. Also checked: the reworked coda about farmor's glasskåp introduces no new defensible reading of any option here, since it concerns the cabinet's afterlife in town and touches neither the set nor the admission criterion.
